Flow Matching with Uncertainty Quantification and Guidance Juyeop Han juyeop@mit.edu Affiliation: MIT Lukas Lao Beyer llb@mit.edu Affiliation: MIT Sertac Karaman sertac@mit.edu Affiliation: MIT Abstract Despite the remarkable success of sampling-based generative models such as flow matching, they can still produce samples of inconsistent or degraded quality.
To assess sample reliability and improve sample fidelity, we propose uncertainty-aware flow matching (UA-Flow) , a lightweight extension of flow matching that predicts the velocity field together with heteroscedastic uncertainty.
UA-Flow estimates spatially localized sample uncertainty by propagating velocity uncertainty through the flow dynamics.
The resulting estimates serve as reliability signals that reflect data-manifold support for each generated sample or region.
We further use them to steer generation via uncertainty-aware guidance (UG) and uncertainty-aware classifier-free guidance (UCFG).
Experiments on ImageNet and CIFAR-10 show that UA-Flow’s uncertainty tracks sample fidelity more consistently than element-wise baselines and that these signals also carry information about data-manifold support.
On ImageNet, UG increases precision at the cost of recall and improves FID, while UCFG maintains lower FID than CFG at large guidance scales. 1 Introduction In recent years, sampling-based generative models such as diffusion ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) and flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of domains, most particularly in image and video generation ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Ho et al., 2022 ) as well as in sequential decision-making ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ) .
Despite this progress, these models often produce samples of inconsistent quality.
As a result, using reliably generated samples in downstream applications remains challenging. To address this issue, the uncertainty associated with each generated sample can be interpreted as a measure of the reliability of the generation process.
Several works have explored uncertainty estimation for diffusion-based generative models by adapting techniques from existing uncertainty quantification literature for neural networks ( Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017 ; Kendall and Gal, 2017 ; Ritter et al., 2018 ) .
In sampling-based generative modeling, uncertainty plays two central roles:
(i) it provides a signal for assessing the quality or reliability of individual generated samples,
and (ii) it can guide the generation process to improve sample quality ( De Vita and Belagiannis, 2025 ) .
However, most prior works ( Kou et al., 2023 ; Jazbec et al., 2025 ) primarily focus on the first role, using uncertainty in a post-hoc manner for sample filtering or selection.
Moreover, existing approaches are often domain-specific ( Sun et al., 2023 ; Franchi et al., 2025 ) and quantify uncertainty over conditional inputs ( Berry et al., 2024 ) . We propose uncertainty-aware flow matching (UA-Flow) , a lightweight extension of flow matching that models heteroscedastic uncertainty in the velocity field.
The discrepancy between the learned and true velocity fields is probabilistically modeled as velocity uncertainty.
By propagating this velocity uncertainty through the flow dynamics, UA-Flow provides principled sample-level uncertainty estimates with minimal additional overhead.
Because uncertainty is modeled element-wise at the velocity level of general flow matching, our approach provides spatially localized uncertainty within each generated sample.
Unlike methods that depend on domain-specific adaptations such as the CLIP encoder used by ( Jazbec et al., 2025 ) , this formulation is, in principle, not specialized to a particular data domain.
Moreover, we can use the learned velocity uncertainty for uncertainty-aware guided sampling, which improves generation quality and is not explicitly considered in closely related prior work ( Kou et al., 2023 ; Jazbec et al., 2025 ) .
The deterministic sampling allows us to localize uncertainty to the learned velocity field and propagate it through the dynamics, in contrast to stochastic sampling. We empirically validate the uncertainty estimates produced by our proposed approach in two settings across CIFAR-10, ImageNet-128 and ImageNet-256.
First, we provide evidence that UA-Flow’s uncertainty correlates with sample fidelity and the degree of support from the training data, with higher uncertainty indicating lower fidelity and weaker data support.
In particular, filtering out high-uncertainty samples yields better fidelity-oriented metrics than prior uncertainty-quantification baselines for sampling-based generative models ( Kou et al., 2023 ; De Vita and Belagiannis, 2025 ) .
Moreover, high uncertainty in generated samples or regions is associated with greater distance from the data manifold and higher data rarity.
Second, we use predicted velocity uncertainty to guide sampling through uncertainty-aware guidance (UG) and uncertainty-aware classifier-free guidance (UCFG).
Our experiments show that UG improves precision at the cost of recall and reduces FID on ImageNet.
UCFG improves the best ImageNet FID over fixed CFG and limits degradation at large guidance scales. Max. Stronger guidance yields more class-consistent samples with lower predicted uncertainty. 2 Background Sampling-based generative models and guidance. Sampling-based generative models synthesize data by iteratively transforming samples from a simple base distribution into the data distribution.
Diffusion models implement this transformation through a gradual denoising process ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) .
Flow matching instead learns a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE) whose velocity field transports samples along a prescribed probability path ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ) .
Across both families, guidance modifies the sampling dynamics to favor samples that better satisfy a condition.
Classifier guidance (CG) injects gradients from an external classifier or constraint functions into the sampling update ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Dao et al., 2023 ) , while classifier-free guidance (CFG) extrapolates conditional and unconditional predictions without a separate classifier ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ) .
A practical challenge is that strong guidance can reduce diversity or induce artifacts at high scales, motivating approaches that moderate the effective guidance signal or adapt its strength during sampling ( Saharia et al., 2022 ; Sadat et al., 2024 ) . Uncertainty quantification for neural networks. A common approach to modeling aleatoric uncertainty is heteroscedastic regression, where the network jointly predicts a mean and an input-dependent variance under a Gaussian negative log-likelihood ( Nix and Weigend, 1994 ; Kendall and Gal, 2017 ) .
Epistemic uncertainty is typically approximated via Bayesian-inspired techniques ( Gal and Ghahramani, 2016 ; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017 ; Ritter et al., 2018 ) .
While standard for classification and regression, applying these to sampling-based generative models requires specifying which intermediate quantities are uncertain (e.g., score/velocity or conditional input) and how uncertainty propagates through the sampling dynamics. Uncertainty quantification with sampling-based generative models. Most existing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods for sampling-based generative models are diffusion-centric and can be broadly grouped by where uncertainty is modeled.
Some quantify uncertainty in the conditional input of conditional diffusion ( Berry et al., 2024 ) .
Others develop diffusion-model uncertainty for domain-specific generation and decision-making, including trajectory planning and multi-agent forecasting ( Sun et al., 2023 ; Capellera et al., 2025 ) , as well as text-to-image uncertainty analysis ( Franchi et al., 2025 ) .
A third line targets uncertainty of the generated sample itself.
BayesDiff ( Kou et al., 2023 ) uses Bayesian/Laplace-based estimators ( Daxberger et al., 2021 ) and propagates uncertainty through the diffusion dynamics.
Other methods rely on feature-space likelihoods based on CLIP encoders ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Jazbec et al., 2025 ) , or pixel-wise aleatoric uncertainty for reliability scoring and uncertainty-guided sampling ( De Vita and Belagiannis, 2025 ) .
Despite this progress, flow-matching-specific UQ remains underexplored, even though its deterministic ODE structure enables modeling uncertainty in the learned velocity field and propagating it through the dynamics. 3 Uncertainty-Aware Flow Matching Flow matching learns a time-dependent velocity field that transports samples from a base distribution 𝐱 0 ∼ p 0 \mathbf{x}_{0}\sim p_{0} to data 𝐱 1 ∼ p 1 \mathbf{x}_{1}\sim p_{1} along a prescribed probability path.
We adopt the common affine path 𝐱 t = α t ​ 𝐱 1 + β t ​ 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{x}_{1}+\beta_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0} over time t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] , which induces the conditional distribution p t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 ) p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}) and the corresponding closed-form conditional target velocity u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 ) u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}) ( Lipman et al., 2024 ) . Here, we interpret velocity uncertainty as the time and the state-dependent discrepancy between the learned mean velocity and the true marginal velocity.
If the learned mean exactly recovered the marginal velocity, this discrepancy and the modeled uncertainty would vanish.
In practice, however, various factors, such as finite training data, limited model capacity, and optimization error, produce local velocity errors.
As these errors accumulate along the ODE trajectory, they can divert generated samples away from regions supported by the data distribution.
UA-Flow models these local discrepancies probabilistically and propagates them through the flow dynamics to quantify sample-level uncertainty. 3.1 Probabilistic Velocity Field Modeling UA-Flow aims to learn the mean, u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ∈ ℝ n \bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , and the diagonal variance, ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 ∈ ℝ n (\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , of the velocity field, using the target velocity u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) as supervision.
We use velocity uncertainty to refer to this predicted element-wise variance.
These predictions define a Gaussian velocity model, u t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) = u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) + σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ⊙ ϵ u_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\bar{u}_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})+\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\odot\epsilon with ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and element-wise multiplication ⊙ \odot . For computational efficiency and representational simplicity, we estimate the variance element-wise.
This is common practice in uncertainty quantification for neural networks ( Kendall and Gal, 2017 ) .
We formulate the uncertainty-aware flow matching loss, ℒ UFM ​ ( θ ) \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}}(\theta) , as a Gaussian negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss for the target velocity: ℒ UFM ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 t , p t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ​ [ ( u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) − u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 2 ​ ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 + log ⁡ ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) ] . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})}\Big[\frac{\big(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\big)^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}+\log(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\Big]. (1) All operations in ℒ UFM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}} are applied element-wise.
This convention is used throughout the paper. As in standard flow matching, the target velocity u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) is not directly accessible, and training instead regresses the model to the conditional velocity u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 ) u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}) under p t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 ) p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}) .
Following the same principle, UA-Flow minimizes a conditional uncertainty-aware flow matching loss, denoted by ℒ CUFM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CUFM}} , which reformulates ℒ UFM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}} in terms of the conditional velocity: ℒ CUFM ​ ( θ ) = 𝔼 t , p 1 ​ ( 𝐱 1 ) , p t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 ) ​ [ U t ​ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 1 ) 2 ​ ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 + ( u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) − u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 ) ) 2 2 ​ ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 + log ⁡ ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CUFM}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t,p_{1}(\mathbf{x}_{1}),p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})}\Big[\frac{U_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{1})}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}+\frac{\big(\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})\big)^{2}}{2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}}+\log(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\Big], (2) Here, U t ​ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 1 ) := u ^ t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) 2 − u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 ) 2 U_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{1}):=\hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2}-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})^{2} approximates the exact element-wise correction U t ⋆ ​ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 1 ) := u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) 2 − u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 ) 2 U_{t}^{\star}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{1}):=u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2}-u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1})^{2} .
In the mean squared error objective used for standard flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , the analogous correction is independent of the parameter θ \theta and can therefore be omitted without changing the optimizer.
In our Gaussian NLL objective, however, the correction is weighted by 1 / [ 2 ​ ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 ] 1/[2(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}] and thus depends on the parameter θ \theta . Because the marginal velocity u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) is intractable, we approximate it using the following reweighted mini-batch estimator: u ^ t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) = ∑ b = 1 B u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 , b ) ​ p t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 , b ) ∑ b = 1 B p t ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ 𝐱 1 , b ) . \hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\frac{\sum_{b=1}^{B}u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1,b})p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1,b})}{\sum_{b=1}^{B}p_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1,b})}. (3) Appendix A details the derivation of ℒ CUFM ​ ( θ ) \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CUFM}}(\theta) as an approximation to ℒ UFM ​ ( θ ) \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}}(\theta) and shows that retaining U t ​ ( 𝐱 t , 𝐱 1 ) U_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t},\mathbf{x}_{1}) yields a closer surrogate than setting it to zero, even though u ^ t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) 2 \hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2} is not an unbiased estimator of u t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) 2 u_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})^{2} .
We empirically observe that the correction is largest early in sampling, and larger mini-batches improve its estimate on ImageNet-256 ( Section 4.6.2 ). Remark. UA-Flow can be fine-tuned from a pre-trained flow matching model.
We find that this preserves generation quality as the model learns uncertainty.
For better mean estimates, we use the β \beta -NLL loss ( Seitzer et al., 2022 ) with the factor sg ⁡ [ ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 ​ β ] \mathrm{sg}\!\left[(\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2\beta}\right] for each element-wise NLL term.
Here, sg \mathrm{sg} denotes stop-gradient and β ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \beta\in[0,1] . 3.2 Uncertainty Propagation through Flow Dynamics We aim to estimate the uncertainty of a generated sample from accumulated velocity uncertainty along the flow.
The network predicts the mean and variance u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) \bar{u}_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) and ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 (\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2} of u t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) u_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) .
We first draw the initial state 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{0} from the base distribution p 0 p_{0} .
For each sample, we fix this initial state and set 𝐱 ¯ 0 = 𝐱 0 \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{0}=\mathbf{x}_{0} and Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 0 ] = 𝟎 \mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{0}]=\mathbf{0} .
We then propagate the state mean 𝐱 ¯ t \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t} and variance Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 t ] \mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}] .
The variance describes uncertainty from the Gaussian velocity model for this fixed initial state. We interpret the endpoint mean 𝐱 ¯ 1 \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{1} as the generated sample and the propagated element-wise variance Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 1 ] \mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{1}] as its sample uncertainty map .
The map retains uncertainty for each coordinate.
A sample-level uncertainty score is a scalar derived from this map or from samples of the predicted endpoint distribution. Section 4 specifies the score for each experiment. Both the mean and covariance approximations use the same first-order Taylor expansion about 𝐱 ¯ t = 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐱 t ] \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{t}] : u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) = u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) + J t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ​ ( 𝐱 t − 𝐱 ¯ t ) + O ⁡ ( ‖ 𝐱 t − 𝐱 ¯ t ‖ 2 ) . \bar{u}_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t})=\bar{u}_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+J_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})(\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+O(\|\mathbf{x}_{t}-\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\|^{2}). (4) Here, J t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ∈ ℝ n × n J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} denotes the Jacobian of the mean velocity with respect to the state evaluated at 𝐱 ¯ t \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t} .
The linear term vanishes in expectation, and the higher-order term is neglected to obtain the mean dynamics d ​ 𝐱 ¯ t d ​ t = u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) . \frac{d\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}{dt}=\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}). (5) For variance propagation, we use Euler discretization, 𝐱 t + Δ ​ t = 𝐱 t + u t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ​ Δ ​ t \mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t}=\mathbf{x}_{t}+u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})\Delta t since higher-order solvers would increase analytical complexity and computational cost.
As in BayesDiff ( Kou et al., 2023 ) , we approximate the evolution of the element-wise variance from 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} to 𝐱 t + Δ ​ t \mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t} as Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 t + Δ ​ t ] ≈ Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 t ] + ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ​ Δ ​ t ) 2 + 2 ​ Δ ​ t ​ Cov ​ ( 𝐱 t , u t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) , \mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t+\Delta t}]\approx\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]+(\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\Delta t)^{2}\\
+2\Delta t\mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})), (6) Here, ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ) 2 (\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2} is the predicted velocity variance evaluated at the mean state, and Cov ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , u t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) ∈ ℝ n \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denotes the element-wise covariance between the state and its velocity.
We regard all covariances as element-wise covariances for both computational and spatial tractability in high-dimensional space.
The velocity variance quantifies injected velocity noise, while the state-velocity covariance captures how state uncertainty couples with the local sensitivity of the velocity field. By inserting the linear term from Equation 4 into the element-wise Cov ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , u t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t})) , it is approximated as Cov ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , u t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) ≈ diag ⁡ ( J t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ) ⊙ Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 t ] \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\approx\mathrm{diag}(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}] (7) where J t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) = ∂ u ¯ t θ ∂ 𝐱 t | 𝐱 ¯ t ∈ ℝ n × n J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})=\frac{\partial\bar{u}^{\theta}_{t}}{\partial\mathbf{x}_{t}}\Big|_{\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} denotes the Jacobian of the mean velocity with respect to the state, evaluated at 𝐱 ¯ t \bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t} .
Also, ⊙ \odot represents element-wise multiplication.
Since forming diag ⁡ ( J t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ) \mathrm{diag}(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})) explicitly is intractable in high dimensions, we approximate diag ⁡ ( J t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ) ⊙ Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 t ] \mathrm{diag}(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))\odot\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}] using Hutchinson’s diagonal estimator ( Bekas et al., 2007 ; Dharangutte and Musco, 2023 ) .
Consequently, the covariance Cov ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , u t θ ) \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}) can be estimated as: Cov ⁡ ( 𝐱 t , u t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) ≈ 1 S ​ ∑ i = 1 S ( 𝝈 t x ⊙ 𝐫 i ) ⊙ ( J t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ​ ( 𝝈 t x ⊙ 𝐫 i ) ) \mathrm{Cov}(\mathbf{x}_{t},u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))\approx\frac{1}{S}\sum_{i=1}^{S}(\bm{\sigma}^{x}_{t}\odot\mathbf{r}_{i})\odot(J^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})(\bm{\sigma}^{x}_{t}\odot\mathbf{r}_{i})) (8) with 𝝈 t x = Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 t ] \bm{\sigma}^{x}_{t}=\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{t}]} .
Each 𝐫 i ∈ ℝ n \mathbf{r}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is a Rademacher vector with independent entries drawn uniformly from { − 1 , + 1 } \{-1,+1\} .
Here, S S is the number of Monte Carlo probes. Section H.1 compares the two methods empirically. 3.3 Uncertainty-Aware Guidance for Flow Matching We incorporate the predicted velocity uncertainty into guided sampling by modifying the mean dynamics in Equation 5 .
We present two mechanisms: (i) an uncertainty-based pseudo-likelihood whose gradient is used as a guidance term, and (ii) an adaptive choice of the CFG scale that reduces the predicted variance of the extrapolated velocity. Uncertainty-aware guidance (UG). Standard guidance steers generation toward a condition y y by adding b t ​ w ​ ∇ 𝐱 t ​ log ⁡ p t ​ ( y ∣ 𝐱 t ) b_{t}w\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(y\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}) to the velocity field u t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) u^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) , where w ≥ 0 w\geq 0 is the guidance scale and b t = − β ˙ t ​ β t ​ α t − α ˙ t ​ β t 2 α t b_{t}=-\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}\beta_{t}\alpha_{t}-\dot{\alpha}_{t}\beta_{t}^{2}}{\alpha_{t}} is the path-dependent coefficient for the affine path 𝐱 t = α t ​ 𝐱 1 + β t ​ 𝐱 0 \mathbf{x}_{t}=\alpha_{t}\mathbf{x}_{1}+\beta_{t}\mathbf{x}_{0} Dhariwal and Nichol (2021) ; Lipman et al. (2024) . To bias sampling toward low-uncertainty regions, we define a pseudo-likelihood over the predicted variance given the state, p ~ t ​ ( ( σ t θ ) 2 ∣ 𝐱 t ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( f ⁡ ( ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 ) ) , \tilde{p}_{t}\big((\sigma_{t}^{\theta})^{2}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}\big)\propto\exp\!\big(f((\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2})\big), (9) where the scalar function f f has larger values when the predicted velocity variance is smaller.
Thus, p ~ t \tilde{p}_{t} favors states with low predicted uncertainty.
We substitute ∇ 𝐱 t ​ log ​ p ~ t ​ ( ( σ t θ ) 2 ∣ 𝐱 t ) = ∇ 𝐱 t f ​ ( ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ) ) 2 ) \nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}\log\tilde{p}_{t}\big((\sigma_{t}^{\theta})^{2}\mid\mathbf{x}_{t}\big)=\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{t}}f((\sigma_{t}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}))^{2}) into the classifier-guidance template to obtain the UG mean velocity: u ¯ t , UG θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) = u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) + b t ​ w ​ ∇ 𝐱 ¯ t f ​ ( ( σ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ) 2 ) , \bar{u}_{t,\mathrm{UG}}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})=\bar{u}_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})+b_{t}w\nabla_{\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}}f((\sigma^{\theta}_{t}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2}), (10) which steers the trajectory toward low-uncertainty regions.
In our experiments, we use the negative squared mean of the element-wise predicted variances, f ⁡ ( σ 2 ) = − ( 1 n ​ ∑ i = 1 n σ i 2 ) 2 f(\sigma^{2})=-\big(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}^{2}\big)^{2} . Section H.2 shows that UG is robust to the choice of f f . Uncertainty-aware classifier-free guidance (UCFG). When UA-Flow is trained with classifier-free conditioning, the CFG extrapolated mean velocity is: u ¯ t , CFG θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ∣ y ) = ( 1 + λ ) ​ u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ∣ y ) − λ ​ u ¯ t θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ∣ ∅ ) , \bar{u}_{t,\mathrm{CFG}}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\mid y)=(1+\lambda)\bar{u}_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\mid y)-\lambda\bar{u}_{t}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}\mid\varnothing), (11) where λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 is the CFG scale and ∅ \varnothing denotes the null condition.
In the CFG discussion, conditional and unconditional refer to predictions with class condition y y and null condition ∅ \varnothing , respectively.
The conditional target velocity in Section 3.1 is conditioned on a data endpoint 𝐱 1 \mathbf{x}_{1} . Let σ t , y θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) \sigma_{t,y}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}) and σ t , ∅ θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) \sigma_{t,\varnothing}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}) denote the predicted element-wise standard deviations of the conditional and unconditional velocities, respectively.
For coordinate i i , the variance of the CFG velocity is Var ​ [ u t , CFG θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ y ) ] i = ( 1 + λ ) 2 ​ ( σ t , y , i θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ) 2 + λ 2 ​ ( σ t , ∅ , i θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ) 2 − 2 ​ λ ​ ( 1 + λ ) ​ r i ​ σ t , y , i θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ​ σ t , ∅ , i θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) , \mathrm{Var}\big[u_{t,\mathrm{CFG}}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid y)\big]_{i}=(1+\lambda)^{2}(\sigma_{t,y,i}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2}+\lambda^{2}(\sigma_{t,\varnothing,i}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}))^{2}-2\lambda(1+\lambda)r_{i}\sigma_{t,y,i}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\sigma_{t,\varnothing,i}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t}), (12) where r i r_{i} is the correlation coefficient between the conditional and unconditional velocity components.
The two velocity predictions come from the same network at the same state and differ only in conditioning, motivating strong correlation approximation r i ≈ 1 r_{i}\approx 1 .
Under this approximation, the variance of the CFG velocity is Var ⁡ [ u t , CFG θ ​ ( 𝐱 t ∣ y ) ] ≈ ( ( 1 + λ ) ​ σ t , y θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) − λ ​ σ t , ∅ θ ​ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ) 2 . \mathrm{Var}\big[u_{t,\mathrm{CFG}}^{\theta}(\mathbf{x}_{t}\mid y)\big]\approx\big((1+\lambda)\sigma_{t,y}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})-\lambda\sigma_{t,\varnothing}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big)^{2}. (13) Empirically, the predicted conditional and unconditional mean velocities have Pearson correlation r = 0.993 r=0.993 on ImageNet-256.
We compute this correlation from element-wise values pooled across all sampling steps.
The correlation at every individual step exceeds 0.98 0.98 ( Section G.4 ). For each sample, we choose one scalar λ \lambda to minimize the total predicted variance of the extrapolated velocity.
We cap this scale at λ max \lambda_{\max} to prevent the extrapolated velocity from diverging: λ ∗ = min ⁡ ( λ opt , λ max ) , \lambda^{*}=\min(\lambda_{\mathrm{opt}},\lambda_{\max}), (14) where λ opt = arg ​ min λ ≥ 0 ∑ i = 1 n ( ( 1 + λ ) σ t , y , i θ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) − λ σ t , ∅ , i θ ( 𝐱 ¯ t ) ) 2 . \lambda_{\mathrm{opt}}=\argmin_{\lambda\geq 0}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big((1+\lambda)\sigma_{t,y,i}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})-\lambda\sigma_{t,\varnothing,i}^{\theta}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{t})\big)^{2}. (15) Here, the sum is over the coordinates of one sample.
The closed-form solution for λ opt \lambda_{\mathrm{opt}} is given in Appendix D .
UCFG recomputes λ opt \lambda_{\mathrm{opt}} and λ ∗ \lambda^{*} for each sample at every sampling step, capped by λ max \lambda_{\max} . UCFG and UG can be applied sequentially at each sampling step.
UCFG first returns the guided mean and variance via Equations 11 , 13 and 14 .
UG then computes its gradient from this local guided variance and adds the correction in Equation 10 . 4 Experiments We design experiments to evaluate whether the uncertainty estimated by UA-Flow (i) can be used as a sample-level reliability signal for generated samples , (ii) represents how weakly each generated sample is supported by the dataset manifold ,
and (iii) can be used as a control signal to improve generation via guided sampling .
To assess (i), we filter out high-uncertainty generated images and compare the resulting FID and precision/recall against baseline uncertainty estimation methods ( Section 4.2 ).
To assess (ii), we measure the correlation of the estimated uncertainty with two manifold-based quantities, distance to the data manifold and rarity, and again compare against the baselines ( Section 4.3 ).
To assess (iii), we conduct controlled ablations on uncertainty-aware guidance (UG) ( Section 4.4 ) and uncertainty-aware classifier-free guidance (UCFG) ( Section 4.5 ) under matched sampling settings. 4.1 Experimental Setup We evaluate our method on CIFAR-10 ( Krizhevsky et al., 2010 ) and ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at resolutions 128 × 128 128\times 128 ( ImageNet-128 ) and 256 × 256 256\times 256 ( ImageNet-256 ).
We report the generative quality metrics, Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) and precision/recall ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019 ) , together with the sample-level manifold metrics, distance to the data manifold and rarity ( Han et al., 2023 ) .
FID measures the overall distributional similarity between generated and real images, while precision and recall respectively capture sample fidelity and distributional coverage.
Distance to the data manifold is the feature-space distance from a generated sample to its k k -nearest real neighbor (here, k = 3 k=3 ), and rarity quantifies how atypical a generated sample is with respect to the real data.
Details not described in this subsection are provided in Appendix E . Training and Model Architectures. For CIFAR-10, we use an ADM-based ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) unconditional flow matching model in pixel space.
For ImageNet, we adopt a DiT-based conditional latent flow matching model ( Dao et al., 2023 ) trained on images resized to 128 × 128 128\times 128 and 256 × 256 256\times 256 .
Specifically, we use DiT-B/2 ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) as the backbone and the pretrained autoencoder from Stable Diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) to map RGB images to a latent tensor with downsampling ratio 8 and 4 channels. For CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-128, we first train a vanilla flow matching model and then fine-tune it by adding a variance prediction head.
For ImageNet-256, we fine-tune a pretrained latent flow matching model released in prior work ( Dao et al., 2023 ) . Sampling Process. All image-generation experiments use the second-order Heun’s method solver with 50 sampling steps.
UA-Flow uses Euler updates for uncertainty propagation, as described in Section 3.2 .
For CIFAR-10, we adopt the EDM sampling schedule ( Karras et al., 2022 ) , while for ImageNet we use uniformly spaced time steps.
UG is applied every two sampling steps, whereas CFG and UCFG are applied at every step. Baselines. We compare against BayesDiff ( Kou et al., 2023 ) , Aleatoric Uncertainty (AU) ( De Vita and Belagiannis, 2025 ) , and Generative Uncertainty (GenUnc) ( Jazbec et al., 2025 ) .
As these methods were originally proposed for diffusion models, we adapt them to flow matching by defining uncertainty over the velocity field and propagating it through the flow dynamics.
Implementation details are provided in Section E.2 . UA-Flow + CLIP. We additionally introduce a variant that scores uncertainty in the CLIP embedding space.
Specifically, we draw multiple samples 𝐱 1 , i \mathbf{x}_{1,i} from the predicted distribution 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝐱 ¯ 1 , Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 1 ] ) \mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}_{1},\mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{1}]) and compute the variance of their CLIP embeddings as the sample-level uncertainty score, analogous to GenUnc. 4.2 Filtering Images with High-Uncertainty Figure 2 : Generative quality metrics vs. filtering ratio on ImageNet-256. At each filtering level, high-uncertainty samples are removed and 50k samples are drawn from the remainder for evaluation.
Compared to the element-wise baselines AU ( De Vita and Belagiannis, 2025 ) and BayesDiff ( Kou et al., 2023 ) , UA-Flow achieves lower FID and higher precision after filtering.
UA-Flow + CLIP further matches the CLIP-based scalar reference GenUnc ( Jazbec et al., 2025 ) . We evaluate whether the predicted uncertainty provides a sample-level reliability signal by progressively filtering out high-uncertainty generated samples and tracking changes in FID and precision/recall. (a) CIFAR-10 (pixel space). (b) ImageNet-128 (latent space). (c) ImageNet-256 (latent space). Figure 3 : Uncertainty maps from UA-Flow, AU, and BayesDiff on generated samples. Brighter values indicate higher uncertainty; maps are normalized per image.
UA-Flow localizes high-uncertainty regions, whereas AU often produces inverted patterns and BayesDiff produces noisy maps. Table 1 : Computational cost (TFLOPS) for sampling and uncertainty quantification per image. Vanilla reports sampling cost only. Method CIFAR-10 ImageNet-128 ImageNet-256 Vanilla 4.044 1.112 4.601 AU 5.014 1.379 5.706 BayesDiff 9.201 2.479 10.26 GenUnc 24.32 7.655 31.39 UA-Flow 5.506 1.380 5.761 UA-Flow + CLIP 5.550 2.200 8.916 Uncertainty aggregation for filtering. Filtering requires a single scalar uncertainty score per sample.
GenUnc and UA-Flow + CLIP directly output a scalar in the CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) embedding space, whereas UA-Flow, BayesDiff, and AU produce element-wise uncertainty maps.
For these element-wise methods, we score each sample by the mean of the top 10 % 10\% highest-uncertainty elements of its uncertainty map, suppressing the influence of large low-uncertainty background regions.
This top- 10 % 10\% mean is the empirical Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) at level α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 , CVaR 0.1 ​ ( u ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ u ∣ u ≥ Q 0.9 ​ ( u ) ] \mathrm{CVaR}_{0.1}(u)=\mathbb{E}[u\mid u\geq Q_{0.9}(u)] , a standard tail-risk objective ( Rockafellar et al., 2000 ) .
For UA-Flow and BayesDiff, the uncertainty map is the propagated endpoint variance Var ⁡ [ 𝐱 1 ] \mathrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_{1}] ; AU aggregates velocity variance over late-stage sampling steps ( Section E.2 ).
Following BayesDiff’s protocol, UA-Flow and BayesDiff update uncertainty every four sampling steps, and we use a single Monte Carlo probe ( S = 1 S=1 ) for the covariance estimator in Equation 8 . Section H.1 shows that more probes do not noticeably improve filtering. Filtering procedure. Without any guidance, we generate 100 ​ k 100\mathrm{k} images per dataset (class-conditional uncertainty for ImageNet, unconditional for CIFAR-10), rank them by the sample-level uncertainty score, and progressively remove the top 10 % 10\% up to 50 % 50\% .
At each ratio, metrics are computed on 50 ​ k 50\mathrm{k} randomly drawn images against 50 ​ k 50\mathrm{k} references. Results. UA-Flow filtering induces a precision-recall trade-off ( Figures 2 , 9(a) and 9(b) ): increasing the filter ratio raises precision and lowers recall.
On ImageNet, FID improves after filtering; on CIFAR-10, where the unfiltered FID is already low, FID increases with the filter ratio. Compared to element-wise baselines (AU, BayesDiff), UA-Flow achieves lower FID and higher precision after filtering on ImageNet-128/256.
With AU, recall consistently decreases, while precision either decreases or does not increase significantly.
BayesDiff shows a mild precision-recall trade-off on CIFAR-10 that does not carry over to ImageNet.
Together, these filtering results suggest that neither AU nor BayesDiff provides a consistent signal of sample fidelity across the tested datasets under flow matching.
Qualitatively, Figure 3 shows that UA-Flow’s uncertainty maps localize high-uncertainty regions whereas AU produces largely inverted patterns and BayesDiff produces noisy maps that fail to localize.
Additional latent-space comparisons and an analysis of BayesDiff’s noisy maps are provided in Figures 9 and G.1 . AU has the lowest computational cost, but UA-Flow exceeds it by only 10% on CIFAR-10 and by less than 1% on ImageNet-128/256, while remaining 1.7–1.8 × \times cheaper than BayesDiff ( Table 1 ). GenUnc attains a lower FID than UA-Flow under its default aggregation, but aggregating UA-Flow’s uncertainty in the same CLIP embedding space (UA-Flow + CLIP) recovers a comparable precision-recall trade-off, outperforming GenUnc in FID on ImageNet-128/256 and trailing in FID on CIFAR-10, at 3.5–4.4 × \times less compute ( Table 1 ). 4.3 Correlation of Uncertainty with Manifold Support Filtering shows that uncertainty separates reliable from unreliable samples, but not why it does so.
We therefore test whether higher predicted uncertainty is associated with weaker support from the data manifold.
We quantify manifold support by the distance to the data manifold and by the rarity score, and measure how strongly the predicted uncertainty correlates with each.
When computing the rarity score, we exclude generated samples and patches classified as existing out-of-data manifold. Without any guidance, we generate 5,000 5{,}000 images per dataset and evaluate them against 5,000 5{,}000 reference images.
As in Section 4.2 , uncertainty is updated every four sampling steps.
We use a single Monte Carlo probe ( S = 1 S=1 ) for the covariance estimator in Equation 8 .
We report the Spearman rank correlation ρ \rho between the uncertainty score and each manifold metric, measured at two different levels: sample-wise and patch-wise.
Here, sample-wise refers to one score per image, and patch-wise refers to one score per image patch. Sample-wise correlation. Both metrics are computed for each generated image as a whole and correlated with a single scalar uncertainty per image.
We use the CLIP-space scores, UA-Flow + CLIP and GenUnc, for this comparison, since Section 4.2 shows that the variance of CLIP embeddings tracks sample-level reliability more closely than uncertainty aggregated in pixel or latent space. Patch-wise correlation. A sample-wise score collapses an image to a single scalar, whereas UA-Flow resolves uncertainty spatially across the generated sample.
To test whether this spatial structure correlates with local manifold support, we compute the same two metrics locally.
We divide generated and reference samples into non-overlapping patches.
We use 2 × 2 2\times 2 latent-space patches on ImageNet-128/256 and 4 × 4 4\times 4 pixel-space patches on CIFAR-10.
The uncertainty score of a patch is the sum of its element-wise uncertainty map over the patch elements, so UA-Flow, AU, and BayesDiff are all compared at this granularity. Table 2 : Spearman rank correlation ρ \rho between predicted uncertainty and manifold support. Sample-wise methods produce a single CLIP-space scalar per image, whereas patch-wise methods produce element-wise uncertainty maps and are correlated at the patch level.
Sample-wise, UA-Flow + CLIP is strongest on ImageNet-128 and ImageNet-256, while GenUnc leads on CIFAR-10.
Patch-wise, UA-Flow attains the strongest correlation with both the distance to the data manifold (Dist. to manifold) and the rarity score on every dataset. Sample-wise Patch-wise Dataset Metric GenUnc UA-Flow + CLIP AU BayesDiff UA-Flow CIFAR-10 Dist. to manifold 0.3462 \mathbf{0.3462} 0.2421 0.2421 − 0.5654 -0.5654 0.5064 0.5064 0.6114 \mathbf{0.6114} Rarity 0.3184 \mathbf{0.3184} 0.2183 0.2183 − 0.5603 -0.5603 0.4803 0.4803 0.6066 \mathbf{0.6066} ImageNet-128 Dist. to manifold 0.3579 0.3579 0.3672 \mathbf{0.3672} − 0.3187 -0.3187 0.1340 0.1340 0.4609 \mathbf{0.4609} Rarity 0.3501 0.3501 0.3901 \mathbf{0.3901} − 0.2925 -0.2925 0.1078 0.1078 0.4037 \mathbf{0.4037} ImageNet-256 Dist. to manifold 0.4190 0.4190 0.4426 \mathbf{0.4426} − 0.4719 -0.4719 0.1820 0.1820 0.5404 \mathbf{0.5404} Rarity 0.3995 0.3995 0.4165 \mathbf{0.4165} − 0.4154 -0.4154 0.1422 0.1422 0.4771 \mathbf{0.4771} Results. In the sample-wise setting, UA-Flow + CLIP correlates more strongly with both the distance to the data manifold and the rarity score on ImageNet-128/256, whereas GenUnc leads on CIFAR-10.
To identify the source of this gap, we discard the variance propagation of Section 3.2 on CIFAR-10 and instead draw a velocity from the learned mean and variance at every sampling step, taking the variance of the resulting samples directly as GenUnc does.
The correlations then rise to 0.3524 0.3524 and 0.3282 0.3282 for the distance to the data manifold and the rarity score, above the corresponding GenUnc values of 0.3462 0.3462 and 0.3184 0.3184 .
This comparison suggests that UA-Flow’s learned velocity uncertainty carries information about manifold support that is partly lost through the variance propagation approximations.
Under direct sampling, UA-Flow’s higher endpoint correlations also suggest an advantage over the velocity uncertainty obtained by the last-layer Laplace approximation (LLLA) ( Daxberger et al., 2021 ) used in GenUnc. Apart from this case, UA-Flow-based methods show higher correlations than all baselines.
The positive correlations indicate that higher uncertainty is associated with greater distance from the data manifold and higher rarity.
This supports our hypothesis that the uncertainty of UA-Flow carries information about how weakly each generated sample is supported by the data manifold.
Moreover, the higher patch-wise correlations show that UA-Flow captures this information spatially. 4.4 Uncertainty-Aware Guidance We evaluate UG by sweeping its scale w ∈ [ 0 , 50 ] w\in[0,50] under fixed CFG scales λ ∈ { 0 , 0.25 , 0.5 } \lambda\in\{0,0.25,0.5\} .
Note that UG and CFG are disabled when w = 0 w=0 and λ = 0 \lambda=0 , respectively.
“CFG + UG” first forms the standard CFG mean and its fixed- λ \lambda variance using Equations 11 and 13 , then applies the uncertainty-aware correction in Equation 10 ; it does not use adaptive UCFG.
Thus, Table 3 fixes λ ∈ { 0 , 0.25 , 0.5 } \lambda\in\{0,0.25,0.5\} and sweeps w w to isolate UG under matched CFG strength. Figure 4 : FID, precision, and recall as the UG scale w w varies on ImageNet-256 under fixed CFG scales λ ∈ { 0 , 0.25 , 0.5 } \lambda\in\{0,0.25,0.5\} . Increasing w w generally improves precision while reducing recall.
At nonzero CFG scales, FID reaches a minimum at an intermediate UG strength and then increases. Each panel uses a fixed class label and random seed; columns sweep w ∈ { 0 , 10 , 30 , 50 } w\in\{0,10,30,50\} from left to right. UG trades diversity for fidelity as the guidance strength increases. Increasing w w induces a precision-recall trade-off: precision generally increases while recall decreases, as shown for ImageNet-256 in Figure 4 .
At nonzero CFG scales, FID decreases up to an optimal UG strength and then increases.
On CIFAR-10, where the baseline FID is already low, this trade-off may instead manifest as a slight increase in FID, consistent with the filtering behavior observed in Section 4.2 . Table 3 summarizes generation quality with and without UG under matched CFG scales, reporting the lowest-FID UG configuration for each CFG setting.
We additionally include uncertainty-aware guidance based on AU as a reference baseline.
AU leads to only marginal changes in generation metrics under flow matching, consistent with Section 4.2 where its uncertainty estimates correlate weakly with sample-level fidelity. Figure 5 shows that samples become more class-consistent and have less complex backgrounds as the UG scale increases.
These qualitative changes are consistent with the measured fidelity-diversity trade-off when steering toward low-uncertainty regions.
Overall, guidance based on a pseudo-likelihood derived from predicted velocity uncertainty improves sample fidelity in the tested settings. 4.5 Uncertainty-Aware Classifier-Free Guidance Figure 6 : FID, precision, and recall as a function of the fixed CFG scale λ \lambda or the maximum UCFG scale λ max \lambda_{\max} on ImageNet-256. Rows show CFG, APG, UCFG, and APG+UCFG from top to bottom; columns sweep the fixed scale λ \lambda or adaptive-scale cap λ max \lambda_{\max} over { 1 , 2 , 5 , 10 , 20 } \{1,2,5,10,20\} from left to right.
Compared to CFG and APG at large fixed scales λ \lambda , UCFG and APG+UCFG preserves structure more robustly under large λ max \lambda_{\max} . To observe the effect of UCFG, we compare standard CFG ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2023 ) and APG ( Sadat et al., 2024 ) with their uncertainty-aware counterparts, UCFG and APG+UCFG, respectively.
We sweep the fixed guidance scale λ \lambda for CFG and APG and the cap λ max \lambda_{\max} for UCFG and APG+UCFG.
The sweep covers { 0 , 0.25 , … , 2.0 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 10 , 15 , 20 } \{0,0.25,\ldots,2.0,3,4,5,10,15,20\} on ImageNet-128 and ImageNet-256.
Here, λ max \lambda_{\max} bounds the adaptive scale λ ∗ \lambda^{*} selected from predicted uncertainty. To reduce oversaturation and artifacts, APG applies guidance along the component of the CFG update orthogonal to the conditional velocity.
APG+UCFG adapts APG’s guidance scale to minimize predicted uncertainty using the same mechanism as UCFG.
Implementation details for APG and APG+UCFG are provided in Section E.3 . Results. Figure 6 compares the ImageNet-256 metrics as the guidance parameters λ \lambda and λ max \lambda_{\max} increase, while Table 4 reports the best settings on both ImageNet resolutions.
As the fixed guidance scale λ \lambda increases, recall degrades sharply for both CFG and APG, and precision of CFG also declines at large λ \lambda , leading to a steep increase in FID.
In contrast, recall decreases more gradually for UCFG and APG+UCFG as λ max \lambda_{\max} increases, resulting in only mild FID degradation at large λ max \lambda_{\max} . Figure 7 shows violin plots of λ ∗ \lambda^{*} for UCFG and APG+UCFG, collected every five steps from 1,000 generated samples.
We observe that λ ∗ \lambda^{*} is typically smaller in early sampling steps and becomes larger in later steps.
This pattern suggests that adaptive scaling limits over-guidance while the sample is still coarse, which may help explain the smaller loss of recall at large λ max \lambda_{\max} .
Qualitatively, large λ \lambda in CFG and APG produces oversaturated samples or mode collapse, while UCFG and APG+UCFG preserve global structure with less saturation under large λ max \lambda_{\max} ( Figure 8 ). Finally, Table 4 reports the best-performing configurations (lowest FID) for each method.
UCFG and APG+UCFG achieve lower FID than their respective counterparts, CFG and APG.
APG+UCFG achieves the lowest FID on both ImageNet resolutions, while UCFG and APG also improve over CFG by retaining higher recall at their optimal scales. 4.6 Additional Analyses 4.6.1 Ablations on design choices. We validate the design choices behind our main configurations ( Appendix H ).
Filtering quality changes little across the tested numbers of Hutchinson probes S S , covariance approximations, variance propagation orders, uncertainty update intervals, and top- k % k\% aggregation ratios.
These results support defaults that reduce computation or simplify the approximation.
UG also changes little across the tested functional forms of f ⁡ ( σ 2 ) f(\sigma^{2}) and guidance intervals, supporting application at every two sampling steps.
Without the bias-correction term U t U_{t} in Equation 2 , filtering and UG retain most of their gains, but UCFG no longer surpasses fixed CFG.
This ablation indicates that U t U_{t} is needed for UCFG to outperform fixed CFG in the tested setting. 4.6.2 Bias and Batch-Size Sensitivity of the Correction Estimator. Table 5 : Batch-size sensitivity of the correction estimator on ImageNet-256 latents. The reference replaces the mini-batch estimate with a 65,536 65{,}536 -candidate estimate. Batch size B B Average bias-correction U t U_{t} Recovered Reference − 0.579 -0.579 — 2 − 0.100 -0.100 17.21% 16 − 0.273 -0.273 47.21% 64 − 0.349 -0.349 60.35% 256 − 0.407 -0.407 70.21% 1,024 − 0.454 -0.454 78.32% The correction term U t U_{t} in Equation 2 is formed from the reweighted mini-batch estimate u ^ t ​ ( 𝐱 t ) \hat{u}_{t}(\mathbf{x}_{t}) of Equation 3 .
Squaring that estimate introduces a bias since the surrogate u ^ t 2 \hat{u}_{t}^{2} is biased for u t 2 u_{t}^{2} even when u ^ t \hat{u}_{t} is a consistent proxy for u t u_{t} .
The bias therefore is governed by the mini-batch estimator variance and decreases with the batch size B B ( Appendix A ). Procedure. We quantify this on ImageNet-256 latent features by averaging U t U_{t} across a range of batch sizes B B .
As a reference, we replace the mini-batch estimate with one formed from 65,536 candidates, evaluated on each of 1,024 queries.
Every tested batch size averages 16 independently sampled candidate pools per query. Results. The correction concentrates in the first 10% of forward generation. Its reference magnitude is 0.579 over t ∈ [ 0 , 0.1 ] t\in[0,0.1] , falls to 0.0146 over t ∈ [ 0.1 , 0.2 ] t\in[0.1,0.2] , and is at most 3.60 × 10 − 7 3.60\times 10^{-7} thereafter.
Over t ∈ [ 0.1 , 0.2 ] t\in[0.1,0.2] , it is only 2.32% of the predicted velocity uncertainty, and the error incurred at B = 1,024 B=1{,}024 is 2.16% of the same quantity, so batch size has little absolute effect once t > 0.1 t>0.1 .
This observation is consistent with Bertrand et al. (2026) , finding that the empirical marginal velocity becomes close to the conditional velocity over time in high dimensional space. Table 5 shows that the correction is material over t ∈ [ 0 , 0.1 ] t\in[0,0.1] and that its estimate improves monotonically with the candidate batch size, recovering 17.2% of the reference at B = 2 B=2 and 78.3% at B = 1,024 B=1{,}024 .
The average predicted velocity uncertainty over this interval is 0.310 with the correction, compared with 0.652 without it.
The variance correction also improves the best UCFG configuration from an FID of 4.67 to 4.30, outperforming fixed CFG at 4.48 ( Section H.3 ).
Larger batches therefore sharpen the estimate exactly where the correction is large, while batch size leaves it essentially unaffected over the rest of the trajectory. 4.6.3 Calibration Analysis Table 6 : Calibration of UA-Flow on ImageNet-256 validation images .
Scores before/after post-hoc isotonic calibration at three noise levels t t .
Details and baselines in Section G.3 . Before After t t ECE ↓ \downarrow Brier ↓ \downarrow ECE ↓ \downarrow Brier ↓ \downarrow 0.5 0.1328 0.4771 0.0066 0.0515 0.7 0.0992 0.3281 0.0038 0.0492 0.9 0.0277 0.1009 0.0008 0.0481 Generative models learn a probability distribution rather than predict a target, so there is no fixed ground truth against which to calibrate UA-Flow’s predicted variance.
We therefore use an indirect protocol on ImageNet-256 validation latents ( Section G.3 ): real latents are noised to time t t and recovered by the ODE, treating the clean latent as ground truth for the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Brier score of the predicted endpoint distribution.
Before calibration, both metrics improve monotonically with t t ( Table 6 ).
Post-hoc calibration further reduces both metrics at each tested noise level.
This reduction suggests that isotonic calibration can improve UA-Flow’s predicted endpoint variance under this indirect reconstruction protocol. 4.6.4 Beyond Image Generation. Table 7 : Push-T early termination. Rollouts whose chunk uncertainty exceeds τ \tau are excluded. Excl. % is the excluded fraction of 1,000 1{,}000 rollouts, and Success % (maximum reward > 1.0 >1.0 ) and Mean MaxR are measured over those retained.
Full table in Table 15 . Threshold τ \tau Excl. % Success % ↑ \uparrow Mean MaxR ↑ \uparrow no removal 0.0% 62.7% 0.9514 0.0010 87.8% 91.0 % 0.9702 0.0025 62.9% 77.6% 0.9597 0.0050 29.2% 66.8% 0.9536 0.0075 14.6% 63.6% 0.9536 0.0100 7.9% 63.3% 0.9521 As preliminary evidence that UA-Flow extends beyond images, we evaluate it on three non-image domains: a 2D checkerboard density ( Section I.1 ), a conditional time-series forecasting task ( Section I.2 ), and a Push-T robot policy benchmark ( Section I.3 ).
In all three, the uncertainty scores distinguish retained samples by coverage, prediction error, or rollout success, respectively.
On the time-series task, discarding the top 10 % 10\% most uncertain predictions reduces MSE by 3.8 × 3.8\times ( Table 14 ).
On Push-T, aborting rollouts when chunk-level uncertainty exceeds a threshold τ = 0.001 \tau=0.001 excludes 87.8 % 87.8\% of rollouts and raises the retained success rate from 62.7 % 62.7\% to 91.0 % 91.0\% , with the mean maximum reward rising from 0.9514 0.9514 to 0.9702 0.9702 ( Table 7 ).
These results suggest that UA-Flow can provide reliability signals beyond image generation.
We treat these as preliminary evidence and leave thorough domain-specific studies to future work. 5 Conclusion We propose uncertainty-aware flow matching (UA-Flow), which predicts element-wise heteroscedastic velocity uncertainty and propagates it through deterministic flow dynamics.
This yields per-sample and spatially localized uncertainty for filtering and enables uncertainty-aware guidance (UG) and step-wise adaptive classifier-free guidance (UCFG).
Across CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, UA-Flow’s uncertainty scores correlate with sample fidelity more closely than element-wise baselines; UA-Flow + CLIP is competitive with the scalar CLIP-based baseline at lower computational cost ( Table 1 ).
Moreover, our results show that UA-Flow’s uncertainty reflects the degree to which each generated sample is supported by the data manifold.
UG induces a precision-recall trade-off by steering toward low-uncertainty trajectories, while UCFG mitigates failures of large fixed guidance via adaptive scaling and remains robust under strong guidance.
A key limitation of our formulation is its reliance on simplifying assumptions made for tractability and efficiency, most notably bias-correction term, diagonal variance and first-order Taylor variance propagation. Relaxing these assumptions is left to future work. Broader Impact Statement This work advances uncertainty quantification for sampling-based generative models by explicitly modeling and propagating uncertainty in flow matching dynamics.
By providing per-sample and spatially localized uncertainty estimates, the proposed approach can help practitioners assess the reliability of generated outputs and make more informed decisions when deploying generative models. Potential positive impacts include improved robustness and safety in downstream applications that rely on generative models.
In particular, uncertainty-aware guidance may reduce failure cases caused by overconfident or excessively guided generation. At the same time, as with other advances in generative modeling, improved generation quality and controllability may amplify existing societal risks associated with synthetic data, including misuse, misinformation, or overreliance on automatically generated content.
We emphasize that uncertainty estimates should be used as a complementary reliability signal rather than a guarantee of correctness. Acknowledgments This work is supported by Hyundai Motor Company. Appendix Contents Appendix A Derivation of the Uncertainty-Aware Flow Matching Loss This appendix provides a detailed derivation of the conditional uncertainty-aware flow matching loss ℒ CUFM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CUFM}} by rewriting the unconditional Gaussian negative log-likelihood loss ℒ UFM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}} in terms of conditional flow matching.
The key idea is to express expectations under the marginal distribution p t ​ ( 𝐱 ) p_{t}(\mathbf{x}) using the conditional distribution p t ​ ( 𝐱 ∣ 𝐱 1 ) p_{t}(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{x}_{1}) , which enables tractable training despite the inaccessibility of the marginal velocity.
For notational simplicity, time is uniformly sampled, i.e. t ∼ U ⁡ ( [ 0 , 1 ] ) t\sim U([0,1]) , though any alternative time-sampling distribution could be used. We begin by expanding the uncertainty-aware flow matching loss ℒ UFM \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{UFM}} and decomposing it into four expectation terms, which will later be rewritten under the conditional distribution.
